title: Pagination, worked end to end (3b1b style)

lines.text: Here is a feed. Three tweets per page. You read page one: T1, T2, T3.
While you scroll, a new tweet arrives at the top. Everything slides down one place.
Now you ask for page two: skip three. And T3 arrives twice.
Delete a tweet instead, and one slides past you. You never see it.
One idea for this whole video. Offset remembers a position. A cursor remembers an item.
Positions move. Items don't.
First, offset. The client calls GET /v1/feed, offset 0, limit 50.
The server runs this SQL: order by time, limit 50, offset 0.
The client must remember a number, and add 50 to it each time.
The reply also carries a total. Counting a sharded table is a scatter-gather. It costs more than the page itself.
Page two: offset 50. It breaks, because skip 50 meant one set of rows then, and another now.
The data shifts under the reader.
It also gets slow. Offset 50 reads 100 rows, and throws away 50.
At page 40, it reads 2,000 rows to hand back 50.
Think of a coat on the third hook. Add a hook by the door, and you grab the wrong coat.
Now the cursor. The first call has no cursor. No cursor means start from the top.
The SQL orders by tweet id, and asks for 51 rows, not 50.
The extra row tells you there is another page. Return 50, and set has_more.
The last tweet handed out is 9142. That goes into the cursor.
Inside, it is plain JSON: id 9142. Base64 makes it look meaningless.
The ugliness is the feature. Clients can't depend on its shape, so you can change it later.
Page two hands the blob back untouched. The server decodes it, and adds one line: tweet id below 9142.
That is the only change. An index seek, 51 rows, at any depth.
Now replay the insert. A new tweet lands on top. But older than 9142 still means the same rows. No repeat. No skip.
Sort by timestamp alone, and forty tweets in one millisecond repeat or vanish. So compare time and id as a pair.
Snowflake IDs are time-ordered and unique. So the id alone is the whole cursor.
On the last page, has_more is false. A short page is not the signal. has_more is the contract.
A page can come back short just because rows were filtered out during hydration.
Where does LIMIT belong? On what you return. Never on what you filter by.
The inner query asks: who does u9 follow? The outer query picks the tweets.
LIMIT 51 on the outer query: the 51 newest tweets, from everyone u9 follows.
Put LIMIT 100 on the inner query, and nine hundred accounts silently drop out of the feed.
No error. No warning. Just tweets that never show up.
And admit it: this query is a teaching shape. The real feed is precomputed.
If u9 follows five thousand people, the database scans all their tweets, on every feed open.
IN or JOIN? One question settles it. Do I need any columns from the second table?
If not, it is a membership test. Is this author in the set? Use IN, or EXISTS.
EXISTS is the safest default when you are only filtering. It stops at the first match.
Need followed_since? It lives only in follows. So it has to be a join.
Now the part that bites. A bad migration leaves the same follow row twice.
The JOIN emits that author's tweets twice. IN still returns each tweet once.
One more: if the column can be NULL, never use NOT IN. One NULL returns zero rows.
IN and EXISTS get the same plan. Pick whichever reads more clearly.
So, say it cold.
Offset pagination isn't slow, it's wrong. The feed mutates between page one and page two, so you duplicate and skip rows.
Opaque cursor over the snowflake tweet ID. Correct under inserts, O(1) at any depth.
Positions move. Items don't.
